To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
human CTLs recognize antigens shared between third-party targets and stimulating populations, even when these populations bear no shared SD antigens, and that these antigens are MHC controlled.
human CTLs recognize MHC antigens not detected by serology, and that the MHC antigens recognized by human CTLs are not identical in the two cell populations involved in a CML assay.
the specificity of human cytolytic T lymphocytes (T cells that kill target cells by releasing cytotoxic substances) can be studied by measuring the amount of 51Cr released from radiolabeled cells.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
human CTLs are not restricted in their specificity by the serologically defined MHC antigens, but rather recognize MHC antigens not detected by alloantisera.
CTLs recognize a variety of antigens, some of which are MHC antigens and some of which are non-MHC.
the recognition of MHC antigens is a necessary condition for the recognition of SD antigens by human CTLs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human CTLs can be induced to kill third-party targets unrelated serologically to either stimulating or responding cells, and that the specificity of the cytotoxicity is MHC controlled.
CTLs are capable of recognizing a wide variety of cell surface antigens and are capable of recognizing antigens not detected by alloantisera.
the cytotoxic T cells are specific in that they are not killing autologous cells and that they can be blocked by the appropriate target cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
human CTLs can recognize and kill target cells that are not related to the responding cells.
human cytotoxic T cells are capable of recognizing and killing cells that are not only different from their stimulating cell population but that are not even from the same individual.

human cytotoxic T cells are not only able to recognize serologically defined (or SD) histocompatibility antigens, but are also able to recognize other MHC antigens that do not elicit serologically defined responses.
